extraction: Original embedded image bytes; no cropping or upscaling.

figures.title: Checking the motion budget
figures.caption: Translation-time measurements compare the default and boosted FarmBot settings. I used hardware benchmarking to assess the practical cost of repeating large numbers of interactions.

figures.title: The camera moves with the robot
figures.caption: The wrist-mounted RealSense camera and end effector on the Cartesian gantry. A known offset from the tool connects the camera view to the robot position.

figures.title: Changing the view changes the input
figures.caption: The thesis compares the traditional view with an orthogonal view of the same target. More consistent geometry helps keep visual measurements useful for action selection.

figures.title: The adapted gripper
figures.caption: The articulated printed gripper mounted to the z-axis, with compliant contact surfaces on its fingers. This was the result of several mechanical and material revisions.

figures.title: The calibration setup
figures.caption: The checkerboard and external camera used in the calibration process. This setup illustrates the alignment work that motivated moving to a more stable camera arrangement.

figures.title: Simulation and physical geometry
figures.caption: The corresponding simulated and physical views show why object scale, cropping, and camera geometry must agree before the policy can choose useful actions.

figures.title: Turning the target into a mask
figures.caption: The K-means target map isolates the visible target pixels. The mask provides both a spatial cue for the policy and a way to measure how much of the target is exposed.

figures.title: Three levels of physical clutter
figures.caption: Basic, moderate, and complex block arrangements used to replicate the earlier Grasping the Invisible experiments on the AGGRO platform.

figures.title: Testing the integrated platform
figures.caption: Average moves and the plotted margins for the three clutter types. More complex arrangements required more actions in these replication tests.

figures.title: Stand-off distance affects scale
figures.caption: Views captured at 20, 120, and 220 cm. The changing size of the same target helps explain why matching visual scale matters when transferring the pipeline.

figures.title: What the existing policy would do
figures.caption: Action-value maps from the original GTI pipeline in a physical scene. Each rotated view represents a candidate action orientation; warmer regions indicate higher predicted value.

figures.title: An early attempt to search a larger area
figures.caption: Four workspace views used for a simple scaling heuristic. I compared normalized affordance values across regions, but did not find sufficiently consistent performance to continue with this approach.

figures.title: Automatically creating training scenes
figures.caption: The simulator places structured block arrangements at varied positions and rotations. The camera insets show the observations used to inspect those generated scenes.

figures.title: A search cue when the object is hidden
figures.caption: A pseudo-target region gives the policy a location to investigate even without a complete visible target. In this example, the lower-valued region surrounds a small visible target sliver.

figures.title: Baseline training
figures.caption: The baseline loss trace over 3,000 training iterations. The large early error settles into a comparatively stable range as the policy learns.

figures.title: Fine-tuning with a pseudo-target
figures.caption: The corresponding training trace for GTI fine-tuning plus pseudo-target guidance shows larger oscillations. Training behavior differed even when the policies addressed the same uncovering task.

figures.title: Comparing all six training runs
figures.caption: Loss traces for the six policy variants. These describe learning behavior; the separate evaluation measures whether the trained policies actually uncover the target.

figures.title: Comparing uncovering performance
figures.caption: The original mean-and-error-margin plot from the thesis, comparing the six variants with the original GTI policy. The surrounding discussion also considers how much the policies disturb nearby clutter.

figures.title: Where the baseline policy wants to push
figures.caption: Baseline action-value maps across different clutter arrangements. The repeated rotations visualize candidate push directions rather than a time sequence.

figures.title: Testing guidance under full occlusion
figures.caption: The original GTI and pseudo-policy action maps in the fully occluded setting. These accompany the initial physical feasibility tests, where the search region was supplied manually.
